subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Microcytic Anaemias: Iron Deficiency and Thalassaemia Major

steps.tx: Inadequate dietary iron intake relative to accelerated infant growth velocity represents the leading hematological nutritional disorder worldwide. In toddlers aged six to twenty-four months fed excessive unfortified cow milk, **pediatric iron deficiency anaemia** develops because cow milk contains poor bioavailable iron and induces occult intestinal blood loss. Toddlers present with progressive pallor, irritability, pica (pagophagia for ice or geophagia for clay), and impaired neurocognitive development.
steps.say: Iron deficiency anemia in toddlers is commonly driven by excessive cow milk consumption. Signs include pallor, irritability, pica, and developmental delay.

vis.alt: Peripheral blood smear showing microcytic hypochromic red blood cells with marked anisopoikilocytosis and pencil cells.
vis.caption: Peripheral blood smear demonstrating microcytic hypochromic erythrocytes and elongated pencil cells in iron deficiency. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Evaluation of complete blood counts and red cell indices establishes the microcytic hypochromic morphological pattern. Red blood cell indices demonstrate marked microcytosis with mean corpuscular volume (MCV) below seventy femtolitres and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) below twenty-five picograms. An elevated **red cell distribution width in iron deficiency** (RDW exceeding fifteen percent) reflects wide variation in red cell size (anisocytosis), distinguishing iron deficiency from thalassaemia trait.
steps.say: A high red cell distribution width over fifteen percent reflects marked anisocytosis in iron deficiency. The Mentzer index helps distinguish it from thalassemia trait.

rows: High RDW confirms anisocytosis in IDA
Most accurate body iron stores assay

steps.tx: Biochemical assessment of body iron compartments confirms depleted storage and circulating iron pools. Serum ferritin provides the most specific indirect measure of total-body iron reserves, dropping below twelve micrograms per litre in iron deficiency, though it acts as an acute-phase reactant during systemic infection. Serum iron concentration is depressed, **total iron-binding capacity is elevated**, and transferrin saturation falls profoundly below sixteen percent.
steps.say: Low serum ferritin below twelve nanograms, high total iron-binding capacity, and transferrin saturation below sixteen percent confirm iron deficiency.

left.title: Biochemical Iron Profile
points: Serum ferritin: markedly depressed (<12 ng/mL)
Serum iron: low (<50 mcg/dL)
TIBC: significantly increased (>400 mcg/dL)
Transferrin saturation: profoundly reduced (<16%)

right.title: Therapeutic Oral Iron Trial
points: Elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg/day in 2 to 3 divided doses
Reticulocyte response peaks at 5 to 7 days
Hemoglobin rises by 1 g/dL every 7 to 10 days
Continue for 2 to 3 months after Hb normalizes

steps.tx: Autosomal recessive mutations in the beta-globin gene on chromosome 11 abolish or severely reduce beta-globin chain synthesis. In homozygous infants presenting during the latter half of the first year of life, **beta-thalassaemia major** (Cooley anaemia) results in severe relative excess of unbound alpha-globin chains. These unstable alpha chains precipitate within developing erythroblasts, causing profound intramedullary apoptosis and ineffective erythropoiesis.
steps.say: Beta-thalassaemia major involves absent beta-globin chains, causing unstable alpha chains to precipitate. Severe intramedullary hemolysis causes profound anemia at six months.

vis.alt: Pathophysiological flowchart depicting ineffective erythropoiesis, severe anemia, extramedullary hematopoiesis, and systemic iron overload.
vis.caption: Ineffective erythropoiesis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, and skeletal deformities in beta-thalassaemia major. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Postnatal switching from fetal hemoglobin to adult hemoglobin unmasks the disease phenotype as gamma-chain synthesis wanes. Infants remain healthy for the first two to six months due to protective levels of **fetal hemoglobin in infancy** (HbF containing two alpha and two gamma chains). As physiological HbF declines and defective adult hemoglobin (HbA) fails to form, infants develop severe progressive pallor, failure to thrive, and hepatosplenomegaly.
steps.say: Fetal hemoglobin protects infants for the first six months until gamma-chain synthesis drops. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows high HbF and absent adult HbA.

left.title: Hemoglobin Switching Timeline
points: HbF (alpha2-gamma2) predominates throughout fetal life
Normal decline in HbF begins around 3 to 6 months
In thalassaemia major, HbA (alpha2-beta2) cannot be synthesized
Profound hemolytic anemia emerges at 6 to 9 months

right.title: Hemoglobin Electrophoresis (HPLC)
points: HbF constitutes 90 to 98% of total hemoglobin
HbA is completely absent in beta-zero thalassaemia
HbA2 variable (normal or slightly increased)
Confirms diagnosis prior to starting transfusions

steps.tx: Massive compensatory expansion of erythroid marrow cavities in response to severe anemia produces dramatic skeletal deformities. Severe extramedullary hematopoiesis causes **thalassaemic facies and chipmunk facies**, marked by frontal bossing, maxillary hyperplasia with malocclusion of teeth, depressed nasal bridge, and prominent malar eminences. Skull radiographs display a classic hair-on-end or crew-cut appearance due to widened diploic spaces.
steps.say: Massive bone marrow expansion causes chipmunk facies with maxillary overgrowth and frontal bossing. Skull radiographs display a classic hair-on-end appearance.

rows: Hair-on-end / Crew-cut appearance on skull X-ray
Early initiation of regular transfusion protocol
Calcium, vitamin D, and bisphosphonate support

steps.tx: Regular packed red blood cell transfusion regimens maintain adequate tissue oxygenation and suppress hyperplastic bone marrow. The cornerstone of medical management is **hypertransfusion therapy in thalassaemia**, administering leukoreduced packed red blood cells every three to four weeks to maintain pre-transfusion hemoglobin levels between 9.5 and 10.5 grams per decilitre, preventing facial deformities, cardiomegaly, and pathologic fractures.
steps.say: Hypertransfusion every three to four weeks maintains pre-transfusion hemoglobin above 9.5 grams per decilitre. It suppresses ineffective marrow expansion and supports normal growth.

left.title: Hypertransfusion Protocol Goals
points: Maintain pre-transfusion hemoglobin >=9.5 to 10.5 g/dL
Post-transfusion hemoglobin target 13 to 14 g/dL
Transfuse every 2 to 4 weeks using leukodepleted RBCs
Completely suppresses abnormal extramedullary haematopoiesis

right.title: Transfusional Iron Accumulation
points: Each mL of transfused packed RBCs provides 1.1 mg iron
Human body lacks physiological iron excretion pathway
Iron overload develops after 10 to 20 transfusions
Serum ferritin exceeds 1,000 ng/mL by 2 to 3 years

steps.tx: Repeated transfusions inevitably deposit toxic iron within cardiac myocytes, hepatocytes, and endocrine glands. Initiated after ten to twenty transfusions or when serum ferritin exceeds one thousand nanograms per millilitre, **iron chelation therapy in thalassaemia** prevents fatal cardiac siderosis. Standard oral chelators include deferasirox (twenty to forty milligrams per kilogram daily) and deferiprone, while subcutaneous deferoxamine is used in severe cardiac iron overload.
steps.say: Start iron chelation when serum ferritin exceeds one thousand or after twenty transfusions. Oral deferasirox or deferiprone prevents fatal cardiac siderosis and cirrhosis.
